audit_status.source_base: Hebrew Judges / Shoftim Micah household shrine, silver image, ephod, teraphim, and Levite priest narrative, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for stolen silver and maternal curse, YHWH-dedication attached to image-making, household shrine objects, appointment of a son and then a Levite as priest, Bethlehem-Judah Levite identity, purchased religious service, father-title language, and the repeated no-king/right-in-own-eyes frame.

verses.restored: There was a man from hill country of Ephraim, and his name was Micah.

familiar.text: And there was a man of mount Ephraim, whose name was Micah.

modern.text: Now a man named Micah from the hill country of Ephraim

verses.restored: He said to his mother, The eleven hundred silver taken from you, about which you uttered a curse and spoke it in my hearing—look, the silver is with me; I took it. His mother said, Blessed be my son by YHWH.

familiar.text: And he said unto his mother, The eleven hundred shekels of silver that were taken from thee, about which thou cursedst, and spakest of also in mine ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it. And his mother said, Blessed be thou of the LORD, my son.

modern.text: said to his mother, “The eleven hundred shekels of silver that were taken from you and about which I heard you utter a curse—I have the silver here with me; I took it.” Then his mother said, “Blessed be my son by the LORD!”

verses.restored: He returned the eleven hundred silver to his mother. His mother said, Consecrating, I consecrate the silver from my hand to YHWH for my son, to make a carved image and a cast image; now I return it to you.

familiar.text: And when he had restored the eleven hundred shekels of silver to his mother, his mother said, I had wholly dedicated the silver unto the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a graven image and a molten image: now therefore I will restore it unto thee.

modern.text: And when he had returned the eleven hundred shekels of silver to his mother, she said, “I wholly dedicate the silver to the LORD for my son’s benefit, to make a graven image and a molten idol. Therefore I will now return it to you.”

verses.restored: He returned the silver to his mother, and his mother took two hundred silver and gave it to the metalworker. He made it into a carved image and a cast image, and it was in house of Micah.

familiar.text: Yet he restored the money unto his mother; and his mother took two hundred shekels of silver, and gave them to the founder, who made thereof a graven image and a molten image: and they were in the house of Micah.

modern.text: So he returned the silver to his mother, and she took two hundred shekels of silver and gave them to a silversmith, who made them into a graven image and a molten idol. And they were placed in the house of Micah.

familiar.text: And the man Micah had an house of gods, and made an ephod, and teraphim, and consecrated one of his sons, who became his priest.

modern.text: Now this man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and some household idols, and ordained one of his sons as his priest.

verses.restored: The man went from city, from Bethlehem in Judah, to sojourn wherever he might find a place. He came to hill country of Ephraim, to house of Micah, while making his way.

familiar.text: And the man departed out of the city from Bethlehemjudah to sojourn where he could find a place: and he came to mount Ephraim to the house of Micah, as he journeyed.

modern.text: This man left the city of Bethlehem in Judah to settle where he could find a place. And as he traveled, he came to Micah’s house in the hill country of Ephraim.

verses.restored: Micah said to him, From where do you come? He said to him, I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn wherever I may find a place.

familiar.text: And Micah said unto him, Whence comest thou? And he said unto him, I am a Levite of Bethlehemjudah, and I go to sojourn where I may find a place.

modern.text: “Where are you from?” Micah asked him. “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah,” he replied, “and I am on my way to settle wherever I can find a place.”

modern.text: “Stay with me,” Micah said to him, “and be my father and priest, and I will give you ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions.” So the Levite went in

translation_notes: Micah confesses taking his mother's silver only after hearing her curse. Her immediate blessing appears to reverse or neutralize the curse, showing religion already entangled with fear, property, and household power.

The mother explicitly dedicates the silver to YHWH while commissioning a carved and cast image. The narrative preserves religious mixture and contradiction; it does not authorize persecution, destruction of another community's sacred objects, or contempt for living traditions.
Only two hundred of the eleven hundred silver is said to go to the metalworker. The relation between carved image and cast image, and the location of the remaining silver, require later audit.

Filling the hand is an installation or ordination idiom. Micah first installs a son and later a Levite, revealing private control over priestly office rather than a neutral model of spiritual authority.

The young Levite is economically precarious and seeking somewhere to live. His acceptance of wages, clothing, food, and a father-title must be read within material dependency, not used to shame poor clergy or workers.

Micah treats Levite identity as a guarantee of Divine favor. The chapter exposes spiritual credentialism and purchased legitimacy; it does not teach that clerical status makes a household morally safe.
The refrain about no king and doing what is right in one's own eyes is a literary judgment on social disorder. It does not prove that monarchy, authoritarian rule, or domination is the cure.
safety_note: Do not use Judges 17 to justify religious persecution, icon-smashing, antisemitism, anti-Catholic polemic, or contempt for household spiritual practice. Do not romanticize purchased clergy, dependency-based spiritual authority, or claims that status guarantees blessing. The chapter portrays a household building certainty from money, sacred objects, and a vulnerable religious worker; it does not present coercive authority as faithfulness.
